title: Compassion Benchmark Daily Briefing -- August 1, 2026
headline: A scanner error mixed up two Kyiv strikes a year apart; the benchmark caught it before scoring.
summary: Fifteen governments, cities, universities and one company were reviewed overnight. Fourteen scores were confirmed within the benchmark's five-point range. One proposal moved forward: Uganda's score would fall from 20.3 to 11.9 of 100, crossing from the Developing band into Critical, after the United Nations Human Rights Office described a widening crackdown on dissent. The finding is logged for a decision, not yet applied, so Uganda's published score stays at 20.3. The night's biggest story was the benchmark checking its own inputs. A missile and drone strike hit Kyiv on July 31, and the nightly scan reported 32 people killed. Contemporaneous news reports gave one to three people killed in the city that day. The higher figure matched a different strike, exactly one year earlier, on the same date. The scan also said July was the worst month for civilian deaths in Ukraine since 2022; United Nations monitors had already reported that June was worse. Neither Ukraine nor Kyiv lost points for being attacked -- both were scored only on their own emergency response, which was protective. Two universities, Shanghai Jiao Tong and Fudan, were cleared of a Pentagon research blacklist that describes U.S. policy, not their own conduct. A claimed use of Indian detention powers around a Delhi protest was also dropped, because the order predated the protest by nearly two weeks. Saudi Arabia, Niger, Quezon City and JPMorgan Chase were reviewed again on reports already scored in prior cycles, so their published scores were confirmed rather than counted twice.

pipeline.queueHandling: Fourteen of fifteen assessments confirmed within the five-point range. One proposal was generated: Uganda's score would fall 8.4 points to 11.9, crossing from Developing into Critical, logged for a decision rather than applied. The published score stays at 20.3. The finding builds on a July 26 review that saw the same pattern on lower-tier evidence and did not produce a proposal; a UN Human Rights Office statement dated July 30 raised the evidence to the benchmark's highest tier and is what moved this from a watch item to a formal proposal. Twelve proposals now sit in the queue: Baxter International at 60.9, Guinea-Bissau at 20.3, Becton Dickinson at 54.1, Ecuador at 35.9, Microsoft AI at 81.4, Tunis at 34.4, Uganda at 20.3, Kathmandu at 18.8, Taipei at 81.4, Carnegie Mellon University at 49.2, Portugal at 65.6, and OpenAI at 27.5.

topSignals.title: The Benchmark Caught Its Own Scanner Attaching a Year-Old Death Toll to a New Kyiv Strike
topSignals.whyItMatters: A nightly scan said 32 people died in a July 31 Kyiv strike. That number belongs to a different strike, one year earlier. Catching it kept a wrong number out of two published scores.
topSignals.description: Russia struck Kyiv with missiles and drones overnight into July 31, 2026. The benchmark's automated scan reported 32 people killed and about 180 injured, and called it the deadliest strike on the capital this year. Neither figure held up. Contemporaneous news coverage of the July 31 strike put the death toll in Kyiv itself at one to three people, with about eight to nine killed nationwide; the scan's larger numbers instead match a Kyiv strike from July 31, 2025, exactly one year earlier. A second scan claim also did not hold: it said July 2026 was the worst month for Ukrainian civilian casualties since 2022. United Nations human rights monitors had already reported, two weeks before the scan ran, that June 2026 held that record, with at least 293 people killed and 1,990 injured. Both corrections mattered for two scores, not one: Ukraine and the city of Kyiv are reviewed separately, and both were being checked on the same strike. Neither lost points for being attacked. Ukraine's own State Emergency Service ran rescue operations at damaged buildings, and Kyiv's government opened metro stations as shelters and coordinated first responders. Ukraine's score held at 50 of 100; Kyiv's held at 46.9 of 100. Both remain in the Functional band.

evidence.claim: UN human rights monitors reported that June 2026, not July, was the worst month for civilian casualties in Ukraine since April 2022, with at least 293 people killed and 1,990 injured.
evidence.source: UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (OHCHR)

topSignals.title: Uganda's Score Would Fall Into the Critical Band on a UN Rights Finding -- Proposed, Not Yet Applied
topSignals.whyItMatters: The UN's human rights office says Uganda is silencing critics through disappearance, torture and mass detention. The finding could cut Uganda's score by more than a third, but it is a proposal awaiting a decision, not a published change.
topSignals.description: The UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights said on July 30, 2026 that Uganda's government is cracking down on dissent, expanding the military's role in civilian life and shrinking space for civil society, in a statement High Commissioner Volker Turk summarized: 'Those who dare to speak out are silenced.' The office documented at least 50 opposition figures, five human rights defenders and five journalists subjected to enforced disappearance, torture or arbitrary detention since Uganda's January 2026 elections, and 10 civil society organizations suspended in the same period. A law passed in May 2026, the Protection of Sovereignty Act, allows prison terms of up to 10 years for civic work that receives foreign funding. Human Rights Watch separately reported on July 23 that soldiers seized opposition figure Muwanga Kivumbi the day after a court granted him bail, and held him incommunicado for 13 days. A Human Rights Watch report describing part of this pattern was already reviewed on July 26, 2026 and did not clear the bar for a proposal on its own. The UN office's statement is a higher-authority source describing a wider pattern, which is what moved the finding from a watch item to a formal proposal. If applied, Uganda's score would fall from 20.3 to 11.9 of 100, crossing from the Developing band into Critical. The proposal has not been applied. Uganda's published score remains 20.3.

evidence.quote: Those who dare to speak out are silenced.
evidence.claim: UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk characterized Uganda's post-election crackdown on dissent.
evidence.source: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

evidence.claim: Since Uganda's January 2026 elections, at least 50 opposition leaders and supporters, five human rights defenders and five journalists have been subjected to enforced disappearance, torture or arbitrary detention, and 10 civil society organizations have been suspended.
evidence.source: UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

evidence.claim: Uganda's military seized a senior opposition figure the day after a court granted him bail and held him incommunicado.

topSignals.title: A Pentagon Blacklist Was Screened Out as Evidence About U.S. Policy, Not the Universities It Named
topSignals.whyItMatters: Two Chinese universities were flagged because the U.S. government barred them from defense-funded research. That is a decision about U.S. security policy, not about how either university treats its own students and staff.
topSignals.description: The U.S. Department of Defense added Shanghai Jiao Tong University to a list of 130 foreign institutions barred from Pentagon-funded research on July 23, 2026, an update that also named Fudan University. Fudan was already screened as a false positive on this listing on July 30, 2026. Shanghai Jiao Tong received its first full review this cycle and was screened the same way: a foreign government's national-security funding decision describes that government's own risk calculus, not the university's conduct toward the people it serves, which is the only thing this benchmark measures. Shanghai Jiao Tong's score was confirmed at 23.1 of 100 against a published 22.7, a difference of 0.4. Fudan's score was confirmed unchanged at 28.1. Neither entity's published score moved because of the listing.

topSignals.title: A Claimed Use of Emergency Detention Powers in Delhi Was Dropped Because the Order Predated the Protest
topSignals.whyItMatters: A scan said Indian authorities invoked special detention powers after a protest. The order was actually signed nearly two weeks earlier, as a routine renewal, so it was not counted as a response to the protest.
topSignals.description: Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International both documented excessive force by police against protesters at the Sansad Chalo demonstration in New Delhi on July 20, 2026. A separate claim -- that authorities followed the protest with a new invocation of the National Security Act, a law allowing detention without trial -- did not hold up. The renewal of the Delhi Police Commissioner's National Security Act authority was issued on July 7, 2026 and took effect July 19, one day before the protest, as a routine periodic renewal unconnected to it. Delhi Police said linkage claims were misleading, and lawyers for the protest movement confirmed all those detained had been released. The underlying protest-policing finding was still counted. India was confirmed at 16.9 of 100 against a published 15.6, a small upward difference well below the threshold for a proposal, because the finding had already been reviewed on July 27, 2026 and no new India-attributable evidence emerged. Delhi was confirmed at 28.1 of 100 against a published 32.8, because most of the policing at the protest is carried out by Delhi Police, a force that reports to India's national government, not the city.

evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch documented excessive force used by Indian police against protesters at the July 20, 2026 Sansad Chalo demonstration in New Delhi.
Amnesty International raised serious human rights concerns about the crackdown on peaceful protesters in New Delhi.

topSignals.title: Four Findings Were Reviewed Again on Evidence Already Scored, and None Was Counted Twice
topSignals.whyItMatters: The same overseas reports kept resurfacing in the nightly scan. Reusing the prior scores instead of re-scoring from scratch stopped one event from silently becoming two or three separate score cuts.
topSignals.description: Four of tonight's fifteen reviews turned out to be repeats of evidence already scored in prior cycles. Saudi Arabia was flagged again on the same Human Rights Watch report about the execution of five Ethiopian migrants, already scored on July 31; its prior values were reproduced rather than re-scored, holding it at 7.5 of 100. Niger was flagged for a third time in seven days on one Human Rights Watch report about three years of military rule; its 8.8 of 100 score was reproduced without a third cut. Quezon City was flagged again on the same Commonwealth Avenue arrests already scored on July 31, holding at 19.4 of 100, just 0.3 points below the Critical boundary; no band change was recorded, because the position is a boundary artifact on tier-2 sourcing, not a new finding. JPMorgan Chase's federal discrimination lawsuit, filed by a former employee and disputed by the company, was reproduced unchanged at 54.4 of 100 from its July 29 review. In each case the underlying finding remains on the record, but reviewing the same evidence twice does not lower a score twice.

evidence.claim: Human Rights Watch reported on July 23, 2026 that three years of military rule in Niger has deepened the country's human rights crisis.

methodologyNotes.name: Date Verification Catches Casualty Figures That Belong to a Different Year
methodologyNotes.description: When a scanner-reported casualty or severity figure cannot be corroborated inside the actual evidence window, the benchmark checks it against contemporaneous, dated primary sources before scoring. Tonight the scanner's reported toll for the July 31, 2026 Kyiv strike -- 32 killed, about 180 injured -- matched a separate Kyiv strike from July 31, 2025, one year earlier. The corrected figures left both Ukraine's and Kyiv's scores unchanged, because neither entity's own conduct was in question either way.

methodologyNotes.name: Evidence-Tier Escalation Converts a Watch Item Into a Proposal Without Compounding
methodologyNotes.description: When the same underlying pattern is corroborated by a higher-authority source in a later cycle, the benchmark treats that as new evidence, not a re-litigation of the earlier review. Uganda's July 26 review saw a tier-3 Human Rights Watch report describing military seizures of government critics and did not produce a proposal. A UN Human Rights Office statement of July 30, at the benchmark's highest source tier, widened the documented pattern and raised the reading past the proposal threshold. This is treated as an escalation of one standing finding, not a second, independent downgrade.

methodologyNotes.name: A Foreign Government's Funding Decision Is Not the University's Own Conduct
methodologyNotes.description: The benchmark scores what an institution does to the people it serves, not decisions made about that institution by an outside government. A US Department of Defense research-funding blacklist update named both Shanghai Jiao Tong University and Fudan University this cycle. Both were screened as false positives on attribution: a national-security funding decision by the United States government describes US risk posture, not either university's conduct toward its own students and staff.

methodologyNotes.name: A Detention-Powers Renewal Issued Before a Protest Is Not Evidence About the Protest
methodologyNotes.description: A scanner claim that Indian authorities invoked new detention powers in response to the July 20, 2026 Sansad Chalo protest in New Delhi did not hold up under date verification: the renewal was issued July 7 and took effect July 19, one day before the protest, as a routine periodic renewal. The underlying protest-policing finding was still counted; the false claim about a new invocation was not.

methodologyNotes.name: Repeat Flags on Identical Evidence Are Reproduced, Not Recounted
methodologyNotes.description: When the same news event is surfaced again in a later cycle without new facts, the benchmark reproduces the prior assessment's dimension values rather than re-scoring from scratch, to avoid compounding one piece of evidence into two or more separate score movements. Four of tonight's fifteen reviews were repeats of this kind: Saudi Arabia, Niger (a third repeat in seven days), Quezon City, and JPMorgan Chase.
